sweep_summary: Six title-hits, all Yupik-specific. The three 1985 Krauss-volume chapters (Jacobson, Miyaoka, Leer) are on file in full (ERIC ED398761, good text layer; copied into the cent2127 folder) and were read: Jacobson p.33 matches the catalog's deciding quotation verbatim; Miyaoka pp.55-56 gives the same rightward iambic/regressive system in foot terms and adds a phrase-level 'unit-final' culminative accent (refines, not contradicts); Leer pp.160-162 (not previously listed) restates it as L-to-R iambic foot construction with the final foot unstressed (confirms). Mithun 1996 (SBPL7, on file) contributes Gabas's acoustic study, which restates the Miyaoka/Jacobson/Woodbury rules and finds the rightmost stressed syllable most prominent (pitch > duration > loudness) -- confirms. Mithun 'Exuberant complexity' is actually 2012 Linguistic Discovery 10(1) (fetched sources open, saved): sentence-level prosody, silent on word stress. Woodbury 1987 (Language 63:685-740) could not be opened -- Cambridge Core purchase-only, JSTOR paywalled, archive.org microfilm restricted; its foot rules are known only via Gabas 1996 and Leer 1985 summaries (medium priority to acquire; it is the standard metrical reference but unlikely to change the 'weight' coding). Nothing read contradicts the catalog; Jacobson 1985 remains the deciding source. written at

new_statements.quote: CY foot definition rules. 1. CVCV rule. Working from left to right, search for contiguous pairs of light syllables where the first syllable is open and there is no enclitic boundary between the two syllables, i.e. (C)VCV(C). a. E-deletion rule. If the second syllable has the form Ce, delete the e (thus closing the first syllable). b. Primary iambic foot rule. Otherwise, define the pair of syllables as an iambic foot. 2. Residual foot rule. ... a. Residual iambic foot rule. Define each non-initial pair of light syllables as an iambic foot. b. Monosyllabic foot rule. Define each remaining lone syllable as a monosyllabic foot. On the metrical grid, asterisk the strong node of each non-final foot.
new_statements.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1985. Toward a Metrical Interpretation of Yupik Prosody. In M. Krauss (ed.), Yupik Eskimo Prosodic Systems: Descriptive and Comparative Studies (ANLC Research Papers 7), 159-172. Fairbanks: Alaska Native Language Center.
new_statements.reading: Iterative left-to-right iambic footing over light syllables; heavy syllables and leftover (incl. closed) syllables form monosyllabic feet and are therefore stressed; the word-final foot's head is left unstressed (p. 162: pitch rises to the strong node of the penultimate foot then drops to the unstressed final syllable). This is the metrical form of the weight-sensitive iambic system the catalog already codes from Jacobson 1985 (same volume) and does not change the 'weight' classification.

sources.locator: sec. 3 'CSY and CY rules', pp. 160-162 (PDF pp. 165-167)
sources.note: Metrical restatement of Jacobson's rules: left-to-right iambic feet over light syllables (first open, no enclitic boundary), heavy and stray syllables as monosyllabic feet, the final foot's strong node unasterisked (word-final syllable unstressed), plus 'the most widespread intonation contour for the word is rising pitch until the strong node of the penultimate foot, then a rapid drop in pitch to the word-final syllable (which is unstressed)' (p. 162). Leer says metrical solutions for CY 'do not crucially improve' the linear description (p. 159). Rest of the paper is Alutiiq.

sources.citation: Mithun, Marianne (ed.) 1996. Prosody, Grammar, and Discourse in Central Alaskan Yup'ik. Santa Barbara Papers in Linguistics 7. (Glottolog 18363)
sources.quote: Rhythmic stress is placed as follows: starting from left to right, stress occurs rhythmically on every other syllable. A word-initial syllable is stressed if it is closed and unstressed if it is open. ... A general rule that de-stresses final syllables is postulated ... [sec. 5] The most general observation to be made from the analyzed data is that Yup'ik words show just one prominent (primary) stress, assigned to their last stressable syllables. ... Pitch seems to rank highest in importance, followed by duration and loudness respectively.
sources.locator: Gabas, N. Jr., 'Phonetic correlates of stress in Yup'ik', pp. 17-36; sec. 2-4 (summaries of Miyaoka 1993, Jacobson 1984, Woodbury 1987) and sec. 5 results (txt lines 732-1040)
sources.note: Edited working-papers volume; the only stress paper is Gabas's CECIL acoustic study (135 GCY words, one speaker). It restates the Miyaoka/Jacobson/Woodbury rules (iterative L-to-R rhythmic stress, initial closed syllable stressed, heavy syllables stressed, regressive stress onto a closed syllable, final destressing) and finds the rightmost stressed syllable phonetically most prominent (pitch > duration > loudness). Mithun's own introduction is about intonation-unit transcription, not word stress.

sources.citation: Alden, McKinley & Anja Arnhold. 2022. User's Guide to Central Alaskan Yup'ik Stress Derivation. University of Alberta ERA report, 9 pp. doi:10.7939/r3-4dd8-0b37 (open)
sources.quote: 'In Hayes' (1995) metrical model, Yup'ik stress parameters include that all feet are binary, quantity sensitive, iambic, constructed left-to-right, and iterative, with the foot's head being obligatorily heavy.' Ordered derivation: lexical stress/gemination; iterative iambs L-to-R (codas moraic, CVVC own foot); automatic gemination (C)V.CVV -> (C)VG.GVV; defooting of CVC in double clash; stressed-schwa deletion; clitic incorporation; iambic lengthening of stressed light open syllables; phrase-final destressing. No primary/secondary distinction drawn.

sources.citation: Gabas, Nilson Jr. 1996. Phonetic correlates of stress in Yup'ik. In M. Mithun (ed.), Prosody, Grammar, and Discourse in Central Alaskan Yup'ik (Santa Barbara Papers in Linguistics 7), 17-36. UCSB. (whole volume fetched sources, 226 pp, open)
sources.quote: Small CECIL study (135 isolated words, one speaker): 'The most general observation to be made from the analyzed data is that Yup'ik words show just one prominent (primary) stress, assigned to their last stressable syllables. This observation was initially made by Miyaoka'; conclusion: 'words seem to have just one prominent or primary stressed syllable, which is realized primarily by means of higher pitch'. Supports Miyaoka's rightmost peak (the prule), but is the study Alden & Arnhold 2023 fail to replicate on connected speech.

sources.citation: Miyaoka, Osahito. 1985. Accentuation in Central Alaskan Yupik. In M. Krauss (ed.), Yupik Eskimo Prosodic Systems, 51-76. Fairbanks: ANLC. (Glottolog 682905)
sources.quote: Basically, a foot in CY is either disyllabic and iambic, consisting of a weak syllable followed by a strong syllable, or monosyllabic (except at the end of a phonological unit). ... A trochaic foot (strong syllable followed by weak) does not occur in CY. [3.1] If a phonological unit has two or more accented syllables, the one closest to the end of the unit carries the greatest prominence. This is called "unit-final" accent. ... These apply iteratively, proceeding from left to right. ... Rhythmic accent, which is completely dependent on the syllabic structure of a word, operates progressively (i.e. rightward) from the beginning of the word to the end.
sources.note: Same system as Jacobson, framed in feet: iterative rightward iambic accent, regressive accent onto closed syllables conditioned by boundaries and marked morphemes, monosyllabic (closed) feet; realized by duration (lengthening/gemination), stress and pitch; the last accented syllable of the phonological unit is most prominent ('unit-final accent'). Refines the catalog's 'no primary/secondary hierarchy' by naming a culminative unit-final prominence, but this is phrase-level, not a lexical main-stress rule.

sources.quote: [Cambridge Core abstract] This paper proposes principles to revise the strict 'double articulation' of standard linguistic theory, and define a class of optional rules of postlexical phonology whose output bears meaning. [Woodbury's foot rules as quoted by Gabas 1996: 26] a.) construct an iambic binary foot on σ1σ2. Conditions: i. σ1 and σ2 are light syllables; ii. if word-initial, σ1 is open; iii. if σ1 is closed and σ2 open, σ1σ2 is word-final. b.) otherwise construct a unary foot on unfooted σ1.
sources.locator: pp. 685-740; foot rules at pp. 699-700 per Gabas 1996 (SBPL7 pp. 25-26) and Leer 1985 p. 160 (citing Woodbury 1984b)
sources.note: The fullest theoretical treatment of CAY (Hooper Bay-Chevak) footing, iambic lengthening and phrase-level prosody; cited by StressTyp2 lects 912/913 and by Alden & Arnhold as a source for non-culminativity; would document the 'no primary/secondary distinction' position first-hand.
